subject: physics

items.q: Which statement describes nuclear fission?
items.correct: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, such as a uranium nucleus.
items.misconception: The joining of two light nuclei together to form a single heavier nucleus.
items.why: The words look and sound alike, both appear in the same chapter, and both are described as releasing energy from the nucleus. They are opposite kinds of change. Fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus such as uranium or plutonium. Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
items.random_wrong: The breaking up of a nucleus into all of its separate protons and neutrons.

items.q: An engineer needs a fuel whose nuclei can undergo fission. Which choice is suitable, and for the right reason?
items.correct: Plutonium, because its nucleus is large and unstable.
items.misconception: Helium, because its nucleus is very small and very stable.
items.why: The phrase 'splitting the atom' is used loosely in everyday language, so students assume it applies to atoms in general rather than to particular nuclei. The specification is precise: fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus, with uranium and plutonium as the examples. A small nucleus is not a fission fuel, and neither is a large nucleus that is stable.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen, because its nucleus is the lightest of them all.

items.q: Usually, for fission to occur, what must happen to the unstable nucleus first?
items.correct: It must first absorb a neutron that hits it.
items.misconception: It must be hit hard by a fast-moving electron.
items.why: The snooker-ball picture of collisions is a powerful one, and diagrams showing an arrow hitting a nucleus look like an impact rather than a capture. The specification says the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. The neutron is taken into the nucleus, not bounced off it, and it is a neutron specifically, not an electron or a gamma ray.
items.random_wrong: Nothing: it will shortly split all on its own.

items.q: A sealed sample of uranium is stored on a shelf. Over many years only a very small number of its nuclei split. Why?
items.correct: Spontaneous fission is rare, so almost no nuclei split unaided.
items.misconception: Fission is happening constantly, but far too slowly to detect.
items.why: Students carry over what they learned about radioactive decay, which does happen spontaneously and at random, and assume fission behaves the same way. Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. That is why fission fuel can be stored safely and why a reactor needs neutrons present to keep the reaction going.
items.random_wrong: Uranium nuclei are stable, so they can never undergo fission.

items.q: As well as two smaller nuclei, what does a fission reaction emit?
items.correct: Two or three neutrons, plus gamma rays.
items.misconception: Two or three neutrons, and nothing else.
items.why: Chain reaction diagrams draw the neutrons prominently because they are what continues the reaction, and often leave the gamma rays out altogether. A fission emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. The gamma rays are part of what is emitted at the moment of the split, even when a simplified diagram does not show them.
items.random_wrong: One neutron only, plus alpha particles.

items.q: A uranium nucleus undergoes fission. What is true of the two nuclei produced?
items.correct: They are roughly equal in size, and both smaller than uranium.
items.misconception: One is almost as large as uranium and the other is very small.
items.why: Students meet alpha decay first, where a small alpha particle leaves a nucleus that is almost unchanged, and they map that picture straight onto fission. In fission the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size. Both products are much smaller than the original nucleus. Alpha decay is a different process and is not fission.
items.random_wrong: They are always exactly identical to each other in every way.

items.q: Immediately after a fission, in what forms is the released energy carried away?
items.correct: As kinetic energy of the fission products and as gamma rays.
items.misconception: As gamma rays only; the products themselves are left at rest.
items.why: Chain reaction diagrams draw the neutrons prominently because they are what continues the reaction, and often leave the gamma rays out altogether. A fission emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. The gamma rays are part of what is emitted at the moment of the split, even when a simplified diagram does not show them.
items.random_wrong: As kinetic energy of the two or three emitted neutrons alone.

items.q: Which of the products of a fission reaction have kinetic energy?
items.correct: All of them: both nuclei and every neutron emitted.
items.misconception: Only the neutrons, because only they are moving off.
items.why: Diagrams draw arrows on the neutrons because those are the particles that go on to cause further fissions, so the two nuclei look as though they stay put. All of the fission products have kinetic energy. The two smaller nuclei recoil from each other and move away, and the emitted neutrons move too, so every product is carrying kinetic energy.
items.random_wrong: Only the two smaller nuclei, not the emitted neutrons.

items.q: Which statement best describes how a chain reaction gets going?
items.correct: Neutrons released by one fission are absorbed by other nuclei.
items.misconception: Gamma rays released by one fission split the nuclei around it.
items.why: Chain reaction diagrams draw the neutrons prominently because they are what continues the reaction, and often leave the gamma rays out altogether. A fission emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays. The gamma rays are part of what is emitted at the moment of the split, even when a simplified diagram does not show them.
items.random_wrong: Electrons knocked off the atoms go on to split other nuclei.

items.q: The specification says the neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. Why 'may' rather than 'will'?
items.correct: Some neutrons escape or are absorbed without causing a fission.
items.misconception: Each neutron does cause a fission, but only after a long delay.
items.why: Textbook chain reaction diagrams show every neutron finding a nucleus, because that is the tidiest way to draw the idea of growth. The specification says the neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction. A neutron can escape from the fuel or be absorbed without causing a fission, which is exactly what makes it possible to control the reaction.
items.random_wrong: Only one neutron is ever released, so the reaction cannot spread.

items.q: In a nuclear reactor the chain reaction is controlled. What is the purpose of controlling it?
items.correct: To control the energy released by the reaction.
items.misconception: To stop the chain reaction from happening at all.
items.why: 'Control' is often heard as 'restrain' or 'shut down', and safety language around reactors reinforces that reading. The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor to control the energy released. The reaction continues; what is controlled is its rate, and therefore the rate at which energy is released.
items.random_wrong: To stop the fuel from emitting any gamma rays.

items.q: What is the essential difference between a nuclear reactor and a nuclear weapon?
items.correct: In a weapon the chain reaction is uncontrolled.
items.misconception: A weapon uses a fuel a reactor cannot use at all.
items.why: Students expect a dramatic difference in outcome to come from a dramatic difference in material, rather than from how the same reaction is managed. The difference the specification draws is control. In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled to control the energy released; in a weapon the chain reaction is uncontrolled, so the energy is released all at once.
items.random_wrong: In a reactor the chain reaction is stopped entirely.

items.q: A diagram of fission shows a large labelled circle for a uranium nucleus, with a small circle arriving at it from the left. What does the small circle represent?
items.correct: A neutron being absorbed by the nucleus.
items.misconception: An electron being fired at the nucleus.
items.why: The snooker-ball picture of collisions is a powerful one, and diagrams showing an arrow hitting a nucleus look like an impact rather than a capture. The specification says the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron. The neutron is taken into the nucleus, not bounced off it, and it is a neutron specifically, not an electron or a gamma ray.
items.random_wrong: A light nucleus about to fuse with it.

items.q: In a chain reaction diagram, one fission at the top releases two neutrons, and each neutron is absorbed and causes a further fission. How many fissions are shown in the third row?
items.correct: 4 fissions
items.misconception: 2 fissions
items.why: Students think of a chain as a line of single links, one after another, which suggests one event leading to one more. Read the diagram from the neutrons. One fission emits two or three neutrons, and each neutron that is absorbed causes a further fission, so the number of fissions per row multiplies rather than staying the same.

items.q: Which statement describes nuclear fusion?
items.correct: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
items.misconception: The joining of two heavy nuclei to form a lighter nucleus.
items.why: Students associate large nuclei with nuclear energy because uranium is the example they meet first, and carry that association into fusion. Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus. It is the light nuclei that fuse; heavy unstable nuclei are what undergo fission.
items.random_wrong: The splitting of one heavy nucleus into two lighter ones.

items.q: Two light nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus. How does the mass of the new nucleus compare with the total mass of the two light nuclei?
items.correct: Slightly less: some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
items.misconception: Exactly the same: mass can never be lost or gained in any change.
items.why: Conservation of mass is taught firmly for chemical reactions and for everyday physical changes, and students apply it to nuclear changes without exception. In fusion some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus has slightly less mass than the total of the two light nuclei. This is a nuclear change, and it is where the energy of the radiation comes from.
items.random_wrong: Slightly more, because energy had to be supplied to force them together.

items.q: When a uranium nucleus undergoes fission, what does it split into?
items.correct: Two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, plus two or three neutrons and gamma rays.
items.misconception: Splitting the nucleus means it comes apart into all its separate protons and neutrons.
items.why: Students picture the nucleus as a bag of loose particles, so 'splitting' suggests the bag bursting and spilling every particle out. The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size. Those pieces are still nuclei, each holding many protons and neutrons together. Only two or three individual neutrons are emitted.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What radiation is emitted at the moment of fission?
items.correct: Gamma rays, along with two or three neutrons.
items.misconception: Fission emits alpha and beta particles, because that is what radioactive substances give out.
items.why: Alpha, beta and gamma are learned together as 'the three radiations', so students reach for the whole set whenever a nucleus changes. The specification is specific about fission: two or three neutrons plus gamma rays are emitted. Alpha and beta emission belong to radioactive decay, which is a different nuclear change.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the two nuclei produced by a fission identical to each other?
items.correct: No. They are roughly equal in size, not necessarily the same.
items.misconception: The nucleus splits exactly in half, so the two nuclei produced must be identical.
items.why: 'Splitting' suggests cutting something down the middle, and 'roughly equal' is read as a polite way of saying 'equal'. The specification says the two smaller nuclei are roughly equal in size. 'Roughly' is doing real work here: the split is not an exact halving and the two products need not be the same.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the energy released in a nuclear power station come from?
items.correct: It is released by the fission reaction when nuclei split.
items.misconception: The uranium fuel is burned, like coal in a coal-fired station, and burning it releases the energy.
items.why: The word 'fuel' and the phrase 'burnt-up fuel rods' come from everyday and industrial language, and the rest of the power station really does behave like a conventional one. Energy is released by the fission reaction itself, when a large unstable nucleus splits. No chemical burning is involved; that is why so much energy comes from so little fuel.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a chain reaction diagram, are the neutrons drawn in a row the same thing as the fissions in that row?
items.correct: No. The neutrons leaving one row are absorbed to cause the fissions of the next row.
items.misconception: Every small circle in the diagram is one fission, so counting the neutrons in a row gives the number of fissions in it.
items.why: Both neutrons and fissions are drawn as small repeated symbols, and students count symbols rather than tracking what each one stands for. Label the diagram as you read it. A fission is a nucleus splitting; the neutrons it emits then travel on and cause the fissions of the following row, so a row of four neutrons produces up to four fissions, not four more neutrons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two light nuclei have to be pushed together very forcefully to fuse. Does that make the new nucleus heavier than the two put together?
items.correct: No. The new nucleus has slightly less mass, as some mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
items.misconception: Energy had to be supplied to force the nuclei together, so that energy is stored in the new nucleus and makes it heavier.
items.why: Students reason that anything put into a process must show up inside the product, and mass is the only property of the product they can point to. Fusion releases energy overall: some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation, so the heavier nucleus formed has slightly less mass than the two light nuclei that joined together.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
